Interactive module

Java Fundamentals

How Java actually runs your code — types, objects, collections and exceptions — built around one order-and-inventory system you carry from the first example to the last.

Basic Java 21 LTS 6–8 hours Updated August 2026

Start here

How to use this module

Work through it at your own pace. Your section checkmarks, quiz answers, flashcard marks and notes are saved in this browser under a key scoped to this file, so closing the tab loses nothing and no other module can overwrite it. Nothing is sent anywhere — this page makes no network requests at all. Press ? at any time for the keyboard shortcuts, and use Reset progress in the sidebar to start over.

Every code sample in this module was compiled and executed against a real JDK 21 as part of the build. If an Expected output block appears under a program, that text is what the program actually printed, not what it ought to print. Where a widget animates execution rather than reporting it, it is labelled Simulated — Java cannot run in a browser, and this module does not pretend otherwise.

One running example

Rather than Foo and bar, everything here is built around a small warehouse system: a Product has a SKU and a price, an Order holds OrderLines, and an InventoryService tracks stock. The same types reappear from the first example to the final lab, so you spend your attention on the language rather than on re-reading the setup.

Your notes

Before you begin

Prerequisites

This module assumes you already program in some language. It does not assume you have written Java. Each item below is something you should already be able to do without looking it up:

Prerequisite skills and what they are needed for
You should already be able to…Because this module…
Read a for loop and an if/else in any C-family languagespends its time on Java's semantics, not on what a loop is
Explain the difference between a variable and the value it holdsleans hard on that distinction for references, ==, and the string pool
Run a command in a terminal and know what a working directory isasks you to run javac and java yourself in the lab
Describe what a function parameter and a return value arebuilds on that for overloading, varargs, and dispatch
Recognise that computers store numbers in a fixed number of bitsshows you exactly what happens when an int runs out of them
What you need installed

A JDK 21 or newer, and nothing else. No IDE is required — every example in this module compiles from the command line.

java -version    # expect: openjdk version "21.x" or newer
javac -version   # the compiler ships with the JDK, not the JRE

If javac is missing but java works, you have a JRE rather than a JDK. Section 1 explains the difference and why it matters.

If you are coming from a specific language
  • Python or JavaScript: the biggest adjustment is static typing and the primitive/object split (sections 2 and 3). Expect the compiler to reject things your old language happily ran.
  • C or C++: there are no pointers you can dereference, no destructors, and no manual free. But there are references, and the distinction between a reference and the object it points to matters constantly.
  • C#: the languages rhyme, but Java's generics are erased rather than reified (section 13), and == on objects never means value equality (section 10).

The contract

Learning objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to do each of the following without reaching for a reference. The final quiz tests exactly these.

  1. Trace a .java file through javac, class loading, and JIT compilation, and say which artefact the JDK, JRE and JVM each own.
  2. Predict the result of integer arithmetic that overflows, of == on boxed values, and of division and modulo on negative operands.
  3. Explain why String is immutable, when two string literals share one object, and what intern() changes.
  4. Choose the right collection for a stated access pattern, and justify it in terms of the cost of the operations you actually perform.
  5. Implement equals and hashCode as a matched pair, and diagnose the failure that follows from overriding only one.
  6. Distinguish checked from unchecked exceptions, and write a try-with-resources block that closes its resources in the correct order.
  7. Resolve an overloaded method call by hand, in the same three phases the compiler uses.
  8. Diagnose a NullPointerException, a ClassCastException from a raw type, and a ConcurrentModificationException from their stack traces and fix each at its cause.
  9. Apply the four access levels correctly, and state which one a member gets when you write no modifier at all.
Deliberately out of scope

Lambdas, streams, concurrency, records, sealed types, pattern matching, the module system and reflection all belong to Java Intermediate. They are mentioned here only where a beginner would otherwise be confused by seeing them in real code. Generics appear, but only as far as declaring and consuming List<Product> — wildcards and erasure edge cases are the advanced module's job.

Section 1

How Java runs your code

Java is neither purely compiled nor purely interpreted, and almost every confusing thing about the toolchain follows from that. Your source is compiled ahead of time into bytecode — a portable instruction set for a machine that does not exist — and then a real machine, the JVM, loads that bytecode, starts interpreting it, and progressively compiles the hot parts to native code while the program runs.

That two-stage design is why a .class file built on your laptop runs unmodified on a Linux server, and why a long-running Java service is often faster after a few minutes than it was at startup.

The mental model

JDK, JRE, JVM — which is which

These three names get used interchangeably in conversation and they are not interchangeable at all. Each one contains the next.

Java Development Kit — everything needed to build Java, which includes everything needed to run it.

  • javac, the compiler that turns .java into .class
  • jar, javadoc, jshell, jlink, and the diagnostic tools (jstack, jmap, jcmd)
  • a complete JRE inside it

Install this one. Since Java 11 there is no separate JRE download from most vendors, and a JDK is what every build tool expects.

Java Runtime Environment — everything needed to run a compiled program, and nothing needed to build one.

  • the JVM itself
  • the standard class library: java.lang, java.util, java.io, and the rest
  • no javac

If java -version works but javac -version says "command not found", you have a JRE. That is the single most common setup problem for people new to Java.

Java Virtual Machine — the specification, and the process that implements it. This is the part that actually executes bytecode.

  • loads and verifies classes, then interprets their bytecode
  • manages the heap and runs the garbage collector
  • JIT-compiles hot methods to native instructions

The JVM is not Java-specific. Kotlin, Scala, Clojure and Groovy all compile to the same bytecode and run on the same machine.

Worked example

The whole cycle, with the smallest program that touches both a reference type and a primitive. Save it as InventoryStart.java — the file name must match the public class name exactly, including case.

javaInventoryStart.java
public class InventoryStart {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String sku = "BOLT-7";
        int onHand = 42;
        System.out.println("SKU " + sku + " has " + onHand + " units on hand.");
        System.out.println("Running on Java " + System.getProperty("java.specification.version"));
    }
}
javac InventoryStart.java   # produces InventoryStart.class
java InventoryStart         # note: no .class extension
Expected output
SKU BOLT-7 has 42 units on hand.
Running on Java 21

That second line is not decoration. This module's build compiled and ran this exact program on the JDK it documents, and captured what it printed — which is how you know the "Java 21" claim on this page is true.

Gotchas that cost beginners an afternoon
  • java InventoryStart.class fails. The launcher takes a class name, not a file name. You will get ClassNotFoundException: InventoryStart.class because it looks for a class literally called class in a package called InventoryStart.
  • The file name must match the public class. class InventoryStart in Start.java is a compile error: class InventoryStart is public, should be declared in a file named InventoryStart.java.
  • main must be exactly that signature. Drop static, or take String instead of String[], and the class compiles fine but the launcher fails at runtime with Main method not found in class InventoryStart. The compiler has no idea you intended that method to be an entry point.
  • "Compiles" and "runs" are separate failures. A missing semicolon is a javac error. A missing class at runtime is a NoClassDefFoundError. Knowing which stage failed halves your debugging time.

Check yourself

Your colleague can run java -version but javac is not found. What do they have, and what should they install?

They have a JRE, not a JDK — the compiler ships only with the JDK. They should install a JDK 21 (or newer) and make sure its bin directory comes first on PATH. On a machine with several Javas installed, java -version and javac -version can even report different versions; if they disagree, PATH is picking the two binaries from different installations.

Why can the same .class file run on Windows, Linux and macOS, when a compiled C program cannot?

Because javac does not target any real CPU. It emits bytecode for the abstract JVM instruction set, and the portability problem is then solved once per platform by shipping a native JVM for each. A C compiler emits instructions for a specific CPU and calls into a specific operating system's ABI, so the binary is bound to both. The cost of Java's approach is that a JVM must be present, and that the first execution of any method is interpreted rather than native.

A service is benchmarked immediately after startup and looks slow, then benchmarked again ten minutes later and looks fast. Nothing was redeployed. Why?

JIT compilation. Every method starts out interpreted. Once a method or loop crosses an invocation threshold the JIT compiles it to optimised native code, using profiling data gathered during interpretation to inline calls and eliminate branches that never fire in practice. This is why JVM benchmarks need a warm-up phase before measurement, and why the first few requests to a freshly deployed service are routinely the slowest ones it will ever serve.

Section 2

Primitives, wrappers, and autoboxing

Java has two kinds of values and the split runs through everything else in the language. A primitive is a raw value of fixed width — int, double, boolean and five others. An object is something on the heap that you reach through a reference. Primitives are not objects, cannot be null, and cannot go into a collection.

That last restriction is why every primitive has a matching wrapper class — Integer for int, Double for double, and so on. Since Java 5 the compiler converts between the two automatically, which is convenient right up to the moment it silently changes what your code means.

The eight primitives

The eight Java primitive types with their widths, ranges, defaults and wrapper classes
TypeBitsRangeDefaultWrapper
byte8−128 … 1270Byte
short16−32,768 … 32,7670Short
int32−2,147,483,648 … 2,147,483,6470Integer
long64±9.22 × 10180LLong
float32≈ ±3.4 × 1038, ~7 digits0.0fFloat
double64≈ ±1.8 × 10308, ~15 digits0.0dDouble
char160 … 65535 (unsigned, a UTF-16 code unit)'\u0000'Character
boolean—true / falsefalseBoolean

The defaults column applies to fields and array elements only. A local variable has no default — the compiler refuses to read one before you assign it.

Explore the ranges

What happens past the top of the range

Worked example

Three behaviours that surprise people, in one program: silent integer overflow, the Integer cache, and binary floating point.

javaPrimitives.java
public class Primitives {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        System.out.println("MAX_VALUE     = " + max);
        System.out.println("MAX_VALUE + 1 = " + (max + 1));
 
        Integer a = 127, b = 127;
        Integer c = 128, d = 128;
        System.out.println("127 == 127    -> " + (a == b));
        System.out.println("128 == 128    -> " + (c == d));
        System.out.println("128 .equals   -> " + c.equals(d));
 
        System.out.println("0.1 + 0.2     = " + (0.1 + 0.2));
        System.out.println("as BigDecimal = " + new java.math.BigDecimal("0.1").add(new java.math.BigDecimal("0.2")));
    }
}
Expected output
MAX_VALUE     = 2147483647
MAX_VALUE + 1 = -2147483648
127 == 127    -> true
128 == 128    -> false
128 .equals   -> true
0.1 + 0.2     = 0.30000000000000004
as BigDecimal = 0.3

Every one of those lines is a bug source in real code:

  • max + 1 wraps to the most negative int. No exception, no warning. A quantity counter that overflows just starts reporting negative stock. Use Math.addExact when overflow would be a correctness problem — it throws ArithmeticException instead.
  • 127 == 127 is true but 128 == 128 is false. Integer.valueOf caches boxed values from −128 to 127 and returns the identical object for those; outside that range it allocates a new one each time. == on wrappers compares references, so the answer changes with the magnitude of the number. This is the single most notorious autoboxing trap.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3. Neither operand is exactly representable in binary floating point, so the sum lands slightly high. Never use double for money — use BigDecimal constructed from a String, or count in integer minor units (cents).
Autoboxing gotchas
  • Unboxing null throws. Map<String,Integer> stock; int n = stock.get("MISSING"); compiles fine and throws NullPointerException at runtime, because get returned null and the compiler inserted .intValue() on it. The stack trace points at the assignment, not at the map.
  • Boxing in a hot loop allocates. Integer total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) total += i; creates a million Integer objects, because each += unboxes, adds, and reboxes. Declaring total as int makes it roughly an order of magnitude faster and allocation-free.
  • Overload resolution changes. Given both remove(int) and remove(Object) on List<Integer>, list.remove(1) removes the element at index 1, while list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the value 1. The compiler prefers the primitive overload without widening or boxing.

Check yourself

1.What does this print?

Integer x = 1000;
Integer y = 1000;
System.out.println(x == y);
System.out.println(x.equals(y));

B. 1000 is outside the Integer cache range of −128…127, so each boxing allocates a separate object and == compares two different references — false. equals compares the wrapped values, so it is true.

A would be right if the value were ≤ 127 — that inconsistency is exactly the trap. C inverts the two operators. D is wrong because the code is perfectly legal; that is the problem with it.

2.An inventory counter is declared int onHand and reaches 2,147,483,647. One more unit arrives and onHand++ runs. What happens?

C. Java uses two's-complement arithmetic that wraps around. Adding 1 to the largest int gives the smallest one, with no diagnostic of any kind.

A is what Math.addExact(onHand, 1) would do, and is what you want here. B is saturating arithmetic, which Java does not do. D never happens implicitly on assignment back into an int — the arithmetic is performed in 32 bits and the result truncated.

Section 3

Strings, immutability, and the pool

String is a normal class, not a primitive — but it gets three privileges no other class has: a literal syntax, the + operator, and a JVM-managed pool of shared instances. Understanding all three is the difference between writing correct string code and writing string code that works by accident.

The foundation is immutability. A String's contents can never change after construction. Every method that looks like it modifies a string — toUpperCase, trim, replace, concat — returns a new string and leaves the original untouched.

The mental model

Worked example

javaStrings.java
public class Strings {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String a = "BOLT-7";
        String b = "BOLT-7";
        String c = new String("BOLT-7");
        String d = c.intern();
 
        System.out.println("a == b        -> " + (a == b));
        System.out.println("a == c        -> " + (a == c));
        System.out.println("a.equals(c)   -> " + a.equals(c));
        System.out.println("a == d        -> " + (a == d));
 
        String s = "BOLT";
        s.concat("-7");
        System.out.println("after concat  : " + s);
        System.out.println("reassigned    : " + s.concat("-7"));
    }
}
Expected output
a == b        -> true
a == c        -> false
a.equals(c)   -> true
a == d        -> true
after concat  : BOLT
reassigned    : BOLT-7

Lines 12–13 are the immutability trap in its purest form. s.concat("-7") computes a new string and throws it away, because nothing captured the return value. s still refers to "BOLT". Every string method behaves this way.

Never compare strings with ==

== asks "are these the same object?". For strings you almost always want "do these hold the same characters?", which is equals. Literal comparison happens to work because of pooling, which makes the bug invisible in tests and fatal in production — a string read from a file, a socket, a database or Scanner is never pooled, so == returns false for characters that are plainly identical. Use a.equals(b), or Objects.equals(a, b) when either side may be null.

Watch the pool

String identity Simulated ← → to step
Source
String a = "BOLT-7";
String b = "BOLT-7";
String c = new String("BOLT-7");
String d = c.intern();
 
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a == c);
System.out.println(a == d);
References
Standard output

Building strings efficiently

Because strings are immutable, concatenating in a loop allocates a new object on every iteration and copies everything so far. For n appends that is O(n²) work. StringBuilder keeps a mutable char buffer and appends in amortised O(1).

String report = "";
for (OrderLine line : order.lines()) {
    report += line.sku() + ",";   // allocates a new String every iteration
}

With 10,000 lines this copies roughly 50 million characters. It is the classic reason a report endpoint that was fine in testing falls over on a large order.

StringBuilder report = new StringBuilder();
for (OrderLine line : order.lines()) {
    report.append(line.sku()).append(',');
}
String result = report.toString();

One buffer, grown geometrically, converted to a String exactly once at the end.

String label = "SKU " + sku + " x" + qty;

Leave this alone. A + chain in a single expression is compiled into one efficient concatenation, so hand-rolling a StringBuilder here makes the code worse and no faster. The rule is about loops, not about +.

More string gotchas
  • split takes a regex, not a literal. "1.2.3".split(".") returns an empty array, because . matches any character. You need split("\\.") or split(Pattern.quote(".")).
  • trim() and strip() differ. trim() removes characters ≤ U+0020 only; strip() (Java 11+) is Unicode-aware and removes things like non-breaking space. Prefer strip() for user input.
  • equalsIgnoreCase beats toLowerCase().equals(…). The latter allocates and, in a Turkish locale, lowercases I to a dotless ı — a real internationalisation bug. If you must change case for comparison, pass Locale.ROOT.
  • length() counts UTF-16 code units, not characters. An emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane counts as 2. Use codePointCount when you mean user-visible characters.

Check yourself

1.A SKU read from a CSV file is compared to a literal with == and the comparison fails, even though printing both shows BOLT-7. Why?

C. Only compile-time literals and explicitly interned strings live in the pool. Anything constructed at runtime — from I/O, concatenation of non-constants, substring, or new String — is a fresh object, so == compares two different references and returns false.

A is a plausible separate bug, but it would also make equals fail, and the printed output would usually reveal it. B is invented — length is irrelevant. D is wrong: a String in memory has no encoding you can observe; encoding applies when converting to and from bytes.

2.What is printed?

String sku = "BOLT-7";
sku.toLowerCase();
sku.replace('-', '_');
System.out.println(sku);

B. Both method calls return new strings that are immediately discarded. sku is never reassigned, and the object it points to cannot change, so it still holds the original characters.

A assumes both calls mutate in place. C and D each assume one of them does. To get bolt_7 you must capture the results: sku = sku.toLowerCase().replace('-', '_');. Modern compilers will warn about ignoring the return value of a pure method — pay attention to that warning.

Section 4

Operators and precedence

Most of Java's operators do what you would guess. The handful that do not are responsible for a disproportionate share of quiet, wrong-answer bugs: integer division that truncates, % that returns negatives, and + that changes meaning as soon as a String enters the expression.

Precedence, highest first

Java operator precedence from highest to lowest, with associativity
TierOperatorsAssociativity
1() [] . x++ x-- (postfix)left → right
2++x --x +x -x ! ~ (cast) newright → left
3* / %left → right
4+ -left → right
5<< >> >>>left → right
6< <= > >= instanceofleft → right
7== !=left → right
8–10& then ^ then |left → right
11&&left → right
12||left → right
13? :right → left
14= += -= *= /= %= …right → left

You do not need to memorise this. You need to recognise the three rows that bite — tier 3 above tier 4, tier 7 below tier 6, and && above || — and reach for parentheses everywhere else.

Evaluate an expression

Step through the evaluation

Worked example

javaOperators.java
public class Operators {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("7 / 2        = " + (7 / 2));
        System.out.println("-7 / 2       = " + (-7 / 2));
        System.out.println("-7 % 2       = " + (-7 % 2));
        System.out.println("floorMod     = " + Math.floorMod(-7, 2));
        System.out.println("7 / 2.0      = " + (7 / 2.0));
 
        System.out.println("2 + 3 + \"!\"  = " + (2 + 3 + "!"));
        System.out.println("\"!\" + 2 + 3  = " + ("!" + 2 + 3));
 
        int i = 2;
        System.out.println("i++ + ++i    = " + (i++ + ++i));
        System.out.println("i is now     = " + i);
 
        int total = 0, count = 0;
        System.out.println("avg guarded  = " + (count > 0 && total / count > 5));
    }
}
Expected output
7 / 2        = 3
-7 / 2       = -3
-7 % 2       = -1
floorMod     = 1
7 / 2.0      = 3.5
2 + 3 + "!"  = 5!
"!" + 2 + 3  = !23
i++ + ++i    = 6
i is now     = 4
avg guarded  = false
  • 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. When both operands are integers, the result is an integer and the fraction is discarded. To get a real quotient, make one side floating point: 7 / 2.0, or (double) total / count. Writing (double)(total / count) is too late — the truncation already happened.
  • -7 / 2 is -3, not -4. Java truncates toward zero rather than flooring. -7 % 2 is -1, because the sign of % follows the dividend. If you are using % to wrap an array index, a negative input produces a negative index and an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — use Math.floorMod, which always returns a non-negative result for a positive modulus.
  • 2 + 3 + "!" is 5! but "!" + 2 + 3 is !23. + is left-associative and switches from addition to concatenation the moment one operand is a String. This is why log messages sometimes show id: 12 when you meant id: 3.
  • && short-circuits, and that is load-bearing. The last line never divides by zero, because count > 0 is false and the right operand is not evaluated at all. Swap in & and the same line throws ArithmeticException. The same pattern guards null: if (o != null && o.isPaid()).

Match each operator to its tier

Drag a term onto its slot, or click one then click the other

Which binds tighter in each pair? Place the operator that wins.

All four correct. The consequences: a + b * c multiplies first; a < b == c parses as (a < b) == c; a || b && c parses as a || (b && c); and -x++ parses as -(x++).

Two that the compiler will not save you from
  • Compound assignment hides a cast. byte b = 10; b += 300; compiles, because += performs an implicit narrowing cast. b = b + 300; does not compile. The convenient form is the one that silently truncates.
  • x == y on double is unreliable. Rounding means 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false. Compare with a tolerance — Math.abs(x - y) < 1e-9 — or avoid floating point for the value entirely.

Check yourself

1.An average is computed as int avg = total / count; with total = 7 and count = 2, and reports 3. Which fix produces 3.5?

D. The cast must apply to an operand before the division, so the division is performed in floating point. Casting one side promotes the other automatically.

A still divides two ints — the truncation to 3 happens first, and widening 3 to 3.0 afterwards cannot recover the lost fraction. B is the same mistake made explicit: the parentheses cast the result, not the operand. C does the division correctly but then fails to compile, because double cannot be assigned to int without an explicit narrowing cast.

2.A ring buffer indexes with items[i % items.length]. It works for months, then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -3. What happened, and what is the fix?

B. The message names index -3, so the modulo returned a negative value, which only happens when i is negative. A monotonically increasing int counter that overflows past Integer.MAX_VALUE wraps to a large negative number — which is exactly why this appears after months of uptime rather than in testing. Math.floorMod returns a non-negative result for a positive modulus.

A would give ArithmeticException: / by zero, not a negative index. C is false — the expression inside [] is delimited by the brackets, so precedence is not involved. D is simply not a Java rule.

Section 5

Control flow

The shapes here will be familiar from any C-family language. What is worth your attention is the enhanced for loop, the difference between break and continue when both appear in one loop, and the switch expression — a Java 14+ form that removes the fall-through bug the old statement was famous for.

The five loop forms

Loop forms and when to use each
FormUse when
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)you need the index, or you are stepping by something other than 1
for (T item : collection)you just need each element — the default choice, and the one that cannot go out of bounds
while (cond)the number of iterations is unknown up front
do { … } while (cond)the body must run at least once (menus, retry loops)
Iterator<T> it = …; while (it.hasNext())you need to remove() while iterating — see the gotcha below

Worked example

A picking routine that skips out-of-stock lines and stops once it has enough. Both continue and break appear, and the order in which they are tested changes the result.

javaControlFlow.java
public class ControlFlow {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] skus   = { "BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "CAM-9", "ROD-4", "PIN-2" };
        int[]    onHand = {       12,       0,       7,       0,      31 };
        int      needed = 2;
        int      picked = 0;
 
        for (int i = 0; i < skus.length; i++) {
            if (onHand[i] == 0) {
                System.out.println("skip  " + skus[i] + " (out of stock)");
                continue;
            }
            if (picked == needed) {
                System.out.println("stop  - picked enough");
                break;
            }
            System.out.println("pick  " + skus[i]);
            picked++;
        }
        System.out.println("picked = " + picked);
 
        for (String sku : new String[] { "BOLT-7", "CAM-9", "ZZZ-1" }) {
            String bin = switch (sku.substring(0, 3)) {
                case "BOL" -> "A1";
                case "CAM" -> "B2";
                default    -> "UNSORTED";
            };
            System.out.println(sku + " -> bin " + bin);
        }
    }
}
Expected output
pick  BOLT-7
skip  NUT-3 (out of stock)
pick  CAM-9
skip  ROD-4 (out of stock)
stop  - picked enough
picked = 2
BOLT-7 -> bin A1
CAM-9 -> bin B2
ZZZ-1 -> bin UNSORTED

Notice ROD-4: it is skipped rather than triggering the stop, because the continue on line 11 fires before control ever reaches the break test. Swap the two if blocks and the loop stops one iteration earlier and prints something different. continue jumps to the next iteration; break leaves the loop entirely — and when both are present, the order you test them in is part of the logic.

Watch it iterate

Picking loop Simulated ← → to step
Source
for (int i = 0; i < skus.length; i++) {
    if (onHand[i] == 0) {
        System.out.println("skip  " + skus[i]);
        continue;
    }
    if (picked == needed) {
        System.out.println("stop  - picked enough");
        break;
    }
    System.out.println("pick  " + skus[i]);
    picked++;
}
System.out.println("picked = " + picked);
Locals
Standard output

Switch: statement versus expression

String bin;
switch (prefix) {
    case "BOL": bin = "A1";
    case "CAM": bin = "B2"; break;
    default:    bin = "UNSORTED";
}

The missing break on the "BOL" case means it falls through and bin ends up "B2". The compiler is happy. Every case needing an explicit break, with fall-through as the default, is a design that produces this bug reliably.

String bin = switch (prefix) {
    case "BOL" -> "A1";
    case "CAM" -> "B2";
    default    -> "UNSORTED";
};

Arrow cases do not fall through, the whole thing is an expression that yields a value, and bin can be final. When switching over an enum the compiler also checks exhaustiveness, so adding a new constant turns every unhandled switch into a compile error rather than a silent default. Prefer this form.

Removing while iterating throws
for (OrderLine line : order.lines()) {
    if (line.qty() == 0) order.lines().remove(line);   // ConcurrentModificationException
}

The enhanced for is an Iterator underneath, and the iterator notices the collection changed beneath it. Despite the name, no concurrency is involved — a single thread does this to itself. Use Iterator.remove(), or list.removeIf(line -> line.qty() == 0), which is clearer and does the same thing safely.

Check yourself

1.In the worked example, what changes if the break block is moved above the continue block?

B. On the fourth iteration picked already equals needed. If the break test comes first it fires immediately, so the loop exits at ROD-4 and the out-of-stock message for it is never reached.

A misses that continue skips the rest of the body. C is impossible — picked is only incremented after both guards pass, and stopping earlier cannot increase it. D invents a rule; break may appear anywhere in a loop body.

2.Which of these safely remove zero-quantity lines while walking the list? Select all that apply.

A and C. removeIf is purpose-built and the clearest option. Iterator.remove() is the low-level equivalent — it updates the iterator's own bookkeeping so no modification is detected.

B throws ConcurrentModificationException — the enhanced for hides an iterator that the direct remove invalidates. D does not throw, which makes it worse: removing at index i shifts everything left, the loop then increments i, and the element that moved into that slot is never examined. Two adjacent zero-quantity lines and it silently keeps one. Iterating backwards would fix it, but removeIf is better.

Section 6

Arrays

An array is a fixed-length, contiguous block of same-typed slots. It is the only built-in container in the language — ArrayList and friends are ordinary classes built on top of one. Arrays are objects, so an array variable holds a reference, and length is a field rather than a method.

Three properties cause nearly all array bugs: the length is fixed at creation, indices run from 0 to length - 1, and arrays do not override equals or toString.

Indices and bounds

Where the boundary actually is

Worked example

javaArrayBasics.java
import java.util.Arrays;
 
public class ArrayBasics {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] qty = new int[4];
        System.out.println("defaults      = " + Arrays.toString(qty));
 
        String[] skus = { "BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "CAM-9" };
        System.out.println("length        = " + skus.length);
        System.out.println("last element  = " + skus[skus.length - 1]);
 
        int[][] weekly = new int[3][];
        weekly[0] = new int[] { 5, 3 };
        weekly[1] = new int[] { 9 };
        weekly[2] = new int[] { 1, 1, 4 };
        System.out.println("jagged        = " + Arrays.deepToString(weekly));
 
        int[] grown = Arrays.copyOf(qty, 6);
        System.out.println("copyOf(6)     = " + Arrays.toString(grown));
 
        String[] a = { "BOLT-7" };
        String[] b = { "BOLT-7" };
        System.out.println("a == b        -> " + (a == b));
        System.out.println("a.equals(b)   -> " + a.equals(b));
        System.out.println("Arrays.equals -> " + Arrays.equals(a, b));
    }
}
Expected output
defaults      = [0, 0, 0, 0]
length        = 3
last element  = CAM-9
jagged        = [[5, 3], [9], [1, 1, 4]]
copyOf(6)     = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
a == b        -> false
a.equals(b)   -> false
Arrays.equals -> true

Lines 20–22 are the trap. Arrays inherit equals from Object, so it is pure identity comparison — exactly the same as ==. Two arrays with identical contents are never equals to each other. You need Arrays.equals for one dimension or Arrays.deepEquals for nested arrays. The same applies to printing: System.out.println(skus) gives you something like [Ljava.lang.String;@1b6d3586, which is the type descriptor and an identity hash, not the contents.

The off-by-one, in full

This is the single most common array bug. The loop condition uses <= where it needs <:

javaArrayBounds.java
public class ArrayBounds {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] skus = { "BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "CAM-9" };
        for (int i = 0; i <= skus.length; i++) {
            System.out.println(i + " -> " + skus[i]);
        }
    }
}
Expected output
0 -> BOLT-7
1 -> NUT-3
2 -> CAM-9
Then it throws
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException:
        Index 3 out of bounds for length 3
        at ArrayBounds.main(ArrayBounds.java:5)

Both the printed lines and the exception type above were captured from an actual run during the build. Read the message literally — it names the offending index and the array's length, which together tell you the loop ran exactly one iteration too many.

Prevent it structurally

Use the enhanced for whenever you do not need the index: for (String sku : skus) cannot go out of bounds, because you never write a bound. Reach for the indexed form only when the index is genuinely part of the logic.

Array gotchas
  • length is a field, not a method. array.length but string.length() and list.size(). Three containers, three spellings.
  • An array of objects is an array of nulls. new String[3] gives you three null slots, not three empty strings. Touching one before assigning it throws NullPointerException.
  • Arrays cannot be resized. "Growing" one means allocating a new array and copying, which is what Arrays.copyOf does and what ArrayList does for you automatically.
  • Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size view. Arrays.asList(skus).add("X") throws UnsupportedOperationException, and writes through the list mutate the original array. For an independent, resizable copy use new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(skus)).
  • Cloning is shallow. weekly.clone() copies the outer array of references; both copies still share the same inner arrays. Mutating weekly[0][0] is visible through both.

Check yourself

1.A test asserts two arrays are equal and fails, though both print the same values element by element. Which comparison was used, and what should it be?

C. Arrays never override equals, so the inherited Object.equals runs and compares references. Two distinct arrays are never equal that way regardless of contents.

A has it backwards: Arrays.equals works fine for object element types too — deepEquals is only needed for nested arrays. B contradicts the premise that the elements match. D is invented; sorting matters for binarySearch, not equality.

2.What does new int[3] contain, and what does new String[3] contain?

B. Array elements always get the default value for their type: numeric zero for primitives, false for boolean, and null for any reference type.

A forgets that int is a primitive and cannot hold null. C is the common wrong guess — Java never manufactures empty strings for you, which is why iterating a fresh String[] and calling a method on each element throws NullPointerException. D confuses array elements with local variables; locals must be definitely assigned before use, array elements are zero-initialised by the JVM.

Section 7

Methods, overloading, and varargs

Java dispatches on the compile-time types of the arguments. Which overload runs is decided entirely by javac before your program starts, using a three-phase algorithm. Knowing those phases turns overload puzzles from guesswork into a lookup.

How the compiler picks

Worked example

javaOverloads.java
public class Overloads {
    static String f(int x)     { return "int"; }
    static String f(long x)    { return "long"; }
    static String f(Integer x) { return "Integer"; }
    static String f(Object x)  { return "Object"; }
    static String f(int... x)  { return "varargs"; }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        byte b = 1;
        System.out.println("f(1)           -> " + f(1));
        System.out.println("f(b)  byte     -> " + f(b));
        System.out.println("f(1L)          -> " + f(1L));
        System.out.println("f((Integer) 1) -> " + f((Integer) 1));
        System.out.println("f(1, 2)        -> " + f(1, 2));
        System.out.println("f(\"x\")         -> " + f("x"));
    }
}
Expected output
f(1)           -> int
f(b)  byte     -> int
f(1L)          -> long
f((Integer) 1) -> Integer
f(1, 2)        -> varargs
f("x")         -> Object

Reading those in phase order:

  • f(1) — phase 1 finds f(int) exactly. f(Integer) would need boxing, which phase 1 forbids.
  • f(b) with a byte — no f(byte) exists, but widening byte→int is allowed in phase 1. int is more specific than long, so f(int) wins.
  • f((Integer) 1) — the argument's compile-time type is now Integer, matching f(Integer) exactly in phase 1. The cast changed the answer without changing the value.
  • f(1, 2) — nothing takes two arguments, so phases 1 and 2 find nothing and phase 3 reaches the varargs form.
  • f("x") — only f(Object) accepts a String.
Overloading gotchas
  • Java is pass-by-value, always. For a reference type the reference is copied, so a method can mutate the object you passed but cannot make your variable point somewhere else. Reassigning the parameter inside the method is invisible to the caller.
  • list.remove(1) vs list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)). On a List<Integer> the first removes index 1 and the second removes the value 1, because phase 1 finds remove(int) before boxing is ever considered.
  • Return type is not part of the signature. Two methods differing only in return type do not compile.
  • Varargs must be last, and one per method. f(String... a, int b) is a compile error. Calling f() with no arguments gives an empty array, not null — but f(null) passes null as the array, so a length check throws.
  • Overloading is compile-time; overriding is runtime. They are unrelated mechanisms that beginners routinely conflate. Section 8 covers the runtime half.

Check yourself

1.What does this print?

static void swap(String a, String b) { String t = a; a = b; b = t; }
 
String x = "BOLT-7", y = "NUT-3";
swap(x, y);
System.out.println(x + " " + y);

B. Unchanged. a and b are copies of the references; reassigning them rebinds only the local parameters. The caller's variables still point where they always did. Java has no way to write a working swap for two variables.

A assumes pass-by-reference, which Java does not have for variables. C and D have no basis — the code is valid and nothing becomes null. Note the distinction: had the method called a mutator on the object rather than reassigning the parameter, the caller would see that change.

2.Given f(int), f(Integer) and f(int...), which runs for the call f(7), and why?

A. The literal 7 has compile-time type int, so phase 1 finds f(int) and resolution stops there.

B would require boxing, which phase 1 excludes — it is only reached in phase 2, and phase 2 never runs because phase 1 succeeded. C is true of varargs in general but it is the phase 3 candidate, evaluated last. D is wrong precisely because the phase ordering exists to break these ties deterministically; ambiguity errors happen between two candidates in the same phase.

Section 8

Classes, inheritance, and polymorphism

A class bundles state with the operations allowed on it. Encapsulation means the state is private and the operations enforce the rules, so an object cannot be put into an invalid condition from outside. Everything else in object-oriented Java rests on that.

Polymorphism is the payoff: code written against a supertype runs against any subtype, and the method that actually executes is chosen at runtime from the object's real class — not from the type of the variable holding it. That runtime choice is dynamic dispatch, and it is the exact opposite of the compile-time overload resolution in the previous section.

Worked example

javaDispatch.java
public class Dispatch {
 
    static abstract class Product {
        private final String sku;               // private: nobody outside can corrupt it
        private int priceInCents;
 
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) {
            if (sku == null || sku.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku required");
            if (priceInCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("price must not be negative");
            this.sku = sku;
            this.priceInCents = priceInCents;
        }
 
        String sku() { return sku; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
 
        abstract int shippingInCents();          // no body: every subclass must decide
 
        int totalInCents() { return priceInCents + shippingInCents(); }
    }
 
    static class Bolt extends Product {
        Bolt(int priceInCents) { super("BOLT-7", priceInCents); }
        @Override int shippingInCents() { return 150; }
    }
 
    static class Girder extends Product {
        Girder(int priceInCents) { super("GIRD-1", priceInCents); }
        @Override int shippingInCents() { return 9_500; }
        @Override int totalInCents() { return super.totalInCents() + 250; }  // crane surcharge
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Product[] cart = { new Bolt(80), new Girder(120_000) };
        for (Product p : cart) {
            System.out.printf("%-8s price=%6d ship=%5d total=%6d%n",
                    p.sku(), p.priceInCents(), p.shippingInCents(), p.totalInCents());
        }
 
        Product p = new Girder(100);
        System.out.println("static type is Product, runtime type is " + p.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}
Expected output
BOLT-7   price=    80 ship=  150 total=   230
GIRD-1   price=120000 ship= 9500 total=129750
static type is Product, runtime type is Girder

The loop variable is declared Product, yet each iteration runs a different shippingInCents. The compiler only verified that some shippingInCents() exists on Product; the JVM picked the implementation from the object's actual class. Girder also overrides totalInCents and calls super.totalInCents() to reuse the base calculation before adding its surcharge.

Watch dispatch resolve

Which method runs Simulated ← → to step
Source
Product p = new Girder(120_000);
 
int ship = p.shippingInCents();
 
int total = p.totalInCents();
 
// inside Girder.totalInCents():
//   return super.totalInCents() + 250;
//   -> Product.totalInCents() runs
//      return priceInCents + shippingInCents();
Resolution
Standard output

Abstract class or interface?

abstract class Product {
    private final String sku;           // state
    Product(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
    String sku() { return sku; }        // shared implementation
    abstract int shippingInCents();     // subclass must supply
}
  • May hold instance fields and constructors
  • May have private and protected members
  • A class extends exactly one
interface Shippable {
    int shippingInCents();                                  // implicitly public abstract
    default boolean isFreeShipping() {                      // Java 8+
        return shippingInCents() == 0;
    }
    static Shippable free() { return () -> 0; }
}
  • No instance state — fields are implicitly public static final
  • A class may implement many
  • default methods allow adding behaviour without breaking implementers

Default to an interface. It describes a capability, permits multiple inheritance of type, and keeps implementations free to sit anywhere in the hierarchy.

Reach for an abstract class only when subclasses must share state or constructor logic — as Product does with its validated sku and priceInCents. A common pattern is both: a public interface for the contract, plus an AbstractProduct that implements the tedious parts for subclasses that want them.

Inheritance gotchas
  • Always write @Override. It is optional to the compiler but it turns a typo into a compile error. Without it, shippingInCent() silently becomes a brand-new method and the base implementation keeps running.
  • static methods are hidden, not overridden. They are bound at compile time from the declared type, so a static "override" is dispatched the opposite way to what you expect.
  • Never call an overridable method from a constructor. The subclass override runs before the subclass's own fields are initialised, so it sees them as null or 0.
  • Fields are not polymorphic. Accessing a field through a superclass-typed reference gets the superclass's field. Only methods dispatch dynamically — another reason to keep fields private.
  • Prefer composition to inheritance. extends couples you to the superclass's implementation, and a change there can break you silently. Inherit to be substitutable for a supertype, not merely to reuse code.

Check yourself

1.A subclass declares int shippingInCent() { return 0; } — note the missing s — without @Override. What happens?

C. A differently named method is simply a different method. With an abstract parent you get a clear error about not implementing the abstract member. With a concrete parent you get no diagnostic at all — the inherited body keeps running and your new method is dead code. That silent case is exactly what @Override exists to catch.

A only happens if you wrote @Override. B is wrong: nothing fails at runtime, which is what makes it insidious. D is invented — dispatch matches on exact name and erased parameter types.

2.You need a type shared by Product, GiftCard and ServicePlan — three classes with no common ancestor and no shared fields — expressing only "this can be priced". What should it be?

B. There is no shared state and the three are otherwise unrelated, so this is a capability, not a family. An interface adds the type without constraining anyone's inheritance.

A burns each class's single extends slot on a type carrying no state — and would be impossible if any of them already extends something. C gives up polymorphism entirely: every new type means editing the utility, and dispatch happens at compile time from the declared type, so a Priceable-typed variable would not resolve correctly. D forces an artificial "is-a" between a physical product and a service plan purely to share one method — the classic inheritance-for-reuse mistake.

Section 9

static and initialization order

static means "belongs to the class, not to any instance". A static field exists once no matter how many objects you create; a static method has no this and cannot touch instance state. That single concept explains counters, constants, factory methods, and main itself.

The part worth memorising is when each piece of initialization runs, because the order is fixed, non-obvious, and shows up in interviews and in real "why is this field null?" bugs.

Worked example

javaInitOrder.java
public class InitOrder {
 
    static class Base {
        static { System.out.println("1. Base   static block"); }
        {        System.out.println("3. Base   instance initializer"); }
        Base()  { System.out.println("4. Base   constructor"); }
    }
 
    static class Derived extends Base {
        static { System.out.println("2. Derived static block"); }
        {        System.out.println("5. Derived instance initializer"); }
        Derived() { System.out.println("6. Derived constructor"); }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("-- before any instance exists --");
        new Derived();
        System.out.println("-- second instance --");
        new Derived();
    }
}
Expected output
-- before any instance exists --
1. Base   static block
2. Derived static block
3. Base   instance initializer
4. Base   constructor
5. Derived instance initializer
6. Derived constructor
-- second instance --
3. Base   instance initializer
4. Base   constructor
5. Derived instance initializer
6. Derived constructor

Four things that output tells you:

  • Static initialization is lazy. The static blocks did not run at program start — they ran at the first new Derived(), after the first println. A class is initialized on first active use, not when the JVM boots.
  • The superclass goes first, at both levels. Base's static block before Derived's; Base's instance work before Derived's.
  • Instance initializers run before the constructor body — and after the implicit super() call.
  • Statics run exactly once. The second instance printed only steps 3–6.

Step through it

Initialization order Simulated ← → to step
Source
System.out.println("-- before any instance exists --");
new Derived();
System.out.println("-- second instance --");
new Derived();
JVM state
Standard output

Order of initialization, as a rule

Initialization steps in order, with when each runs
#StepRuns
1Superclass static fields and static blocksOnce, on first active use of the class
2This class's static fields and static blocks
3Superclass instance fields and instance initializersEvery new
4Superclass constructor body
5This class's instance fields and instance initializers
6This class's constructor body

Within a level, fields and initializer blocks run in the order they appear in the source. A field declared below an initializer that reads it will still hold its default value at that point.

Where this bites
  • A constructor calling an overridable method. Step 4 runs the superclass constructor, which may call an overridden method — and that override belongs to a subclass whose fields are not initialised until step 5. The override sees null and 0. Make such methods final or private.
  • static mutable state is shared by everything. A static SimpleDateFormat or a static collection is a data race waiting for a second thread, and a memory leak that never gets collected because the class holds it for the JVM's lifetime.
  • static final primitives and Strings are inlined at compile time. A constant is copied into every calling class's bytecode, so changing it and recompiling only that one class leaves the old value baked into the others.
  • You cannot use this in a static context. "Non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context" almost always means you tried to touch instance state from main.

Check yourself

1.What does this print?

class Config {
    private final String name = describe();
    private final String type = "PRODUCT";
    private String describe() { return "type is " + type; }
    public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(new Config().name); }
}

B. Instance fields initialise top to bottom. When name is computed, type has not been assigned yet and still holds its default of null. Concatenating null into a string yields the four characters null rather than failing.

A assumes declaration order does not matter — swapping the two lines really would produce it. C is the intuitive guess but string concatenation is null-safe; you would only get an NPE if describe called a method on type. D describes the illegal-forward-reference rule, which applies to direct reads in an initialiser, not to reads inside a method the initialiser calls — which is exactly why this compiles and misbehaves.

2.InventoryService keeps private static int totalPicks, incremented in an instance method. Two services are constructed and each picks 3 items. What is totalPicks?

C. A static field belongs to the class. Both instances increment the same storage, so the counts add up to 6.

A describes an instance field — drop static and it would be 3 each. B inverts the real rule: an instance method may freely read and write statics; it is the other direction, static code touching instance state, that is forbidden. D is wrong single-threaded — though with two threads and no synchronisation the count really would become unreliable, since ++ is not atomic. That is a genuine hazard of mutable static state, covered in Java Intermediate.

Section 10

equals, hashCode, toString

Every class inherits these three from Object, and the inherited versions are almost never what you want. equals defaults to reference identity, hashCode to a value derived from the object's identity, and toString to a class name and a hex hash.

The critical rule is that equals and hashCode are one contract, not two methods: if two objects are equals, they must return the same hashCode. Override one without the other and every hash-based collection in the JDK starts giving wrong answers — quietly, with no exception.

See the buckets

A HashSet receiving two equal parts and one different one

Worked example

BadPart below overrides both methods — but derives the hash from a per-instance id that equals never looks at. That is a contract violation, and it fails deterministically.

javaEqualsContract.java
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;
 
public class EqualsContract {
 
    static final class BadPart {
        private static int counter = 0;
        private final String sku;
        private final int id = ++counter;
 
        BadPart(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
 
        @Override public int hashCode() { return id; }   // NOT derived from sku
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            return o instanceof BadPart other && sku.equals(other.sku);
        }
    }
 
    static final class GoodPart {
        private final String sku;
 
        GoodPart(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
 
        @Override public int hashCode() { return sku.hashCode(); }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            if (this == o) return true;
            if (!(o instanceof GoodPart other)) return false;
            return sku.equals(other.sku);
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return "GoodPart[sku=" + sku + "]"; }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<BadPart> bad = new HashSet<>();
        bad.add(new BadPart("BOLT-7"));
        bad.add(new BadPart("BOLT-7"));
        System.out.println("bad  equals    -> " + new BadPart("X").equals(new BadPart("X")));
        System.out.println("bad  set size  -> " + bad.size());
        System.out.println("bad  contains  -> " + bad.contains(new BadPart("BOLT-7")));
 
        Set<GoodPart> good = new HashSet<>();
        good.add(new GoodPart("BOLT-7"));
        good.add(new GoodPart("BOLT-7"));
        System.out.println("good equals    -> " + new GoodPart("X").equals(new GoodPart("X")));
        System.out.println("good set size  -> " + good.size());
        System.out.println("good contains  -> " + good.contains(new GoodPart("BOLT-7")));
        System.out.println("good toString  -> " + new GoodPart("BOLT-7"));
    }
}
Expected output
bad  equals    -> true
bad  set size  -> 2
bad  contains  -> false
good equals    -> true
good set size  -> 1
good contains  -> true
good toString  -> GoodPart[sku=BOLT-7]

Read the first three lines together: the two BadParts are equal, the set still holds both, and looking one up fails. A hash collection computes the hash first and only compares with equals inside the matching bucket — so unequal hashes mean equals is never even called. Omitting hashCode entirely produces the same failure, just non-deterministically, since identity hashes occasionally collide by luck.

The equals contract

For non-null x, y, z: reflexive — x.equals(x); symmetric — x.equals(y) implies y.equals(x); transitive; consistent across repeated calls; and x.equals(null) is always false. Symmetry is the one subclassing breaks: if equals uses getClass() != o.getClass(), a subclass instance is never equal to a base instance; if it uses instanceof, a base instance can be equal to a subclass instance but not the reverse. Declaring value classes final — as above — sidesteps the whole problem.

Build a correct equals

Put these five lines in the right order. Aim for the version that is correct and exits early on the cheapest checks.

  1. 1 return sku.equals(other.sku);
  2. 2 if (this == o) return true;
  3. 3 }
  4. @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { 4
  5. 5 if (!(o instanceof GoodPart other)) return false;

Correct. The identity check first because it is a single pointer comparison and is often true for repeated lookups. Then the instanceof pattern, which handles the wrong type and null in one test — null instanceof Anything is false — and binds other so no cast is needed. Only then the field comparison, which is the expensive part.

Gotchas
  • Wrong parameter type silently overloads. public boolean equals(GoodPart o) does not override anything — Object.equals still wins when a collection calls it. @Override catches this instantly.
  • Never hash on a mutable field. Mutate a key after inserting it into a HashMap and it moves to a bucket nobody will look in. The entry is lost, and it still holds memory.
  • Objects.equals and Objects.hash handle null. Objects.hash(sku, price) is the readable default; for a hot path with one field, sku.hashCode() avoids the varargs array allocation.
  • Write toString for humans, and never put secrets in it. It ends up in logs and exception messages. Tokens, passwords and full card numbers must not.
  • A record gives you all three, correctly, for free. If the class is a transparent carrier of data, use one — Java Intermediate covers them.

Check yourself

1.A Product overrides equals on sku but not hashCode. Two products with the same SKU go into a HashSet. What is most likely observed?

C. Different identity hashes almost always mean different buckets, so equals is never consulted and the duplicate is stored. A lookup with a third equal instance hashes somewhere else again and finds nothing.

A is what you would get if hashCode were also overridden. B never happens — the JDK cannot detect the violation, which is the whole problem. D is self-contradictory: the same hash mismatch that allowed the duplicate also breaks the lookup. Note "most likely" — with luck the two identity hashes land in the same bucket and you get size 1, which is worse still, because the bug then appears only intermittently.

2.Is hashCode() { return 1; } — the same value for every instance — a violation of the contract?

A. The contract only requires that equal objects share a hash code. A constant satisfies that trivially and is therefore correct — just pathologically slow, since a hash map degenerates to a single bucket. (Modern HashMap treeifies large buckets, softening it to O(log n) for comparable keys, but it is still the wrong thing to ship.)

B states the converse, which is not required and cannot be — there are more possible objects than int values, so collisions are unavoidable. C is excellent advice and the practical way to satisfy the contract, but it is not itself the rule. D gets the verdict right and the reasoning wrong: equals is only reached for entries already in the same bucket, so the collisions are precisely what costs you.

Section 11

Exceptions and try-with-resources

An exception unwinds the stack looking for a handler. If none is found the thread dies and the trace is printed. Java splits exceptions into two kinds, and the split is enforced by the compiler rather than by convention.

Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws; the compiler will not let you ignore them. They model conditions a correct program can still hit — a file is missing, a socket drops. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses) need no declaration and model bugs — a null you should have guarded, an argument that violates a documented precondition.

Worked example

javaExceptions.java
public class Exceptions {
 
    static class Resource implements AutoCloseable {
        private final String name;
        Resource(String name) { this.name = name; System.out.println("open  " + name); }
        void use() { System.out.println("use   " + name); }
        @Override public void close() { System.out.println("close " + name); }
    }
 
    static int sneaky() {
        try {
            return 1;
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally runs before the caller sees the value");
        }
    }
 
    static int stockFor(String sku) {
        if (sku == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku must not be null");
        return 42;
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Resource a = new Resource("A"); Resource b = new Resource("B")) {
            a.use();
            b.use();
        }
 
        System.out.println("sneaky() = " + sneaky());
 
        try {
            stockFor(null);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally always runs");
        }
    }
}
Expected output
open  A
open  B
use   A
use   B
close B
close A
finally runs before the caller sees the value
sneaky() = 1
caught: sku must not be null
finally always runs

Two details in that output earn their place:

  • Resources close in reverse order — B then A. They are released like a stack, which is what you need when a later resource depends on an earlier one (a statement opened from a connection, say). This happens whether the block exits normally or by exception, with no finally written by you.
  • finally runs before the caller sees the return value. The return value is computed and set aside, then the finally block runs, then control returns. If a finally block itself returns, it replaces the pending return and discards any in-flight exception — which is why returning from finally is a bug rather than a technique.

Checked or unchecked?

Place each situation on the exception type it should use

The distinction is who is at fault. A missing file is the environment's doing and a correct program must cope — checked. A bad argument, an uninitialised field, and an operation invalid for the current state are all programming errors: the fix is to change the code, not to catch anything. Note the pair IllegalArgument versus IllegalState — the first says "this input is wrong", the second says "this input might be fine later, but not now".

Never swallow an exception
try {
    inventory.reserve(sku, qty);
} catch (Exception e) { }        // the outage you will spend a day finding

An empty catch destroys the only evidence that anything went wrong. If a failure is genuinely expected and ignorable, say so in a comment and log at debug. Otherwise handle it, or wrap it with context and rethrow: throw new InventoryException("reserving " + sku, e) — passing the original as the cause keeps the underlying trace attached.

Gotchas
  • Catch the specific type, and order subclasses first. catch (Exception e) before catch (IOException e) is a compile error — the second is unreachable.
  • The old finally { in.close(); } pattern loses exceptions. If the body threw and close() also throws, the close exception replaces the real one. Try-with-resources instead suppresses the secondary exception and attaches it, retrievable via getSuppressed().
  • Java 14+ gives helpful NPE messages. Instead of a bare line number you get Cannot invoke "Product.sku()" because "<local3>" is null — read it, it names the exact expression.
  • Exceptions are not control flow. Building a stack trace is expensive; using one to exit a loop is slow and obscures intent.
  • Do not catch Error. OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError mean the JVM is in no state to continue.

Check yourself

1.In the worked example, Resource A is opened, then B's constructor throws. What is closed?

B. Try-with-resources tracks what it has successfully acquired. A exists, so it is closed; B never came into being, so there is nothing to close. This is precisely the case hand-written finally blocks get wrong.

A would leak A. C would call close() on a reference that was never assigned — an NPE. D inverts it.

2.A REST handler wraps its whole body in catch (Exception e) { return 200; } to stop 500s appearing in the dashboard. What is the real consequence?

C. The dashboard turns green because the failures stopped being reported, not because they stopped happening. A caller told "200 OK" will not retry, so a reservation that never persisted is simply gone. The metric got healthier and the system got worse.

A mistakes suppressing the signal for handling the problem. B is factually wrong — RuntimeException is a subclass of Exception, so this catches everything except Error. D is closer, and logging is strictly better than not, but the response code is still a lie; the status must reflect what actually happened.

Section 12

Collections: choosing the right one

Three interfaces cover almost everything. List is an ordered sequence that allows duplicates and is addressable by index. Set holds distinct elements. Map associates keys with values. Pick the interface from what your data is, then pick the implementation from how you will use it.

Describe your access pattern

What are you storing?

Cost of the operations you actually perform

Time complexity of common operations by implementation
Typeget by indexcontainsadd at endadd/remove at frontOrdered?
ArrayListO(1)O(n)O(1)*O(n)insertion
LinkedListO(n)O(n)O(1)O(1)insertion
ArrayDeque—O(n)O(1)*O(1)*insertion
HashSet / HashMap—O(1)O(1)*—none
LinkedHashSet / LinkedHashMap—O(1)O(1)*—insertion
TreeSet / TreeMap—O(log n)O(log n)—sorted

* amortised — occasionally a resize copies everything, but averaged over many operations the cost is constant.

LinkedList is almost never the answer

The table says O(1) insertion, which sounds decisive — but to insert at index i you must first walk i nodes, so the real cost is O(n) anyway. Meanwhile ArrayList's O(n) shift is a single System.arraycopy over contiguous memory, which the CPU cache handles roughly an order of magnitude faster than chasing scattered node pointers, and each node costs an extra object header plus two references. LinkedList wins only when you insert through an Iterator you already hold. If you want a queue or a stack, use ArrayDeque.

Worked example

javaCollectionTour.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;
 
public class CollectionTour {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> picks = new ArrayList<>(List.of("NUT-3", "BOLT-7", "NUT-3"));
        System.out.println("list, dupes kept     = " + picks);
 
        Set<String> unique = new HashSet<>(picks);
        System.out.println("hashset size         = " + unique.size());
        System.out.println("linkedhashset        = " + new LinkedHashSet<>(picks));
        System.out.println("treeset, sorted      = " + new TreeSet<>(picks));
 
        Map<String, Integer> onHand = new HashMap<>();
        onHand.put("BOLT-7", 12);
        onHand.put("NUT-3", 0);
        System.out.println("get missing key      = " + onHand.get("NOPE"));
        System.out.println("getOrDefault         = " + onHand.getOrDefault("NOPE", 0));
        System.out.println("containsKey NUT-3    = " + onHand.containsKey("NUT-3"));
 
        onHand.put("BOLT-7", onHand.get("BOLT-7") + 5);
        System.out.println("after restock        = " + onHand.get("BOLT-7"));
 
        try {
            List.of("A", "B").add("C");
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("List.of is immutable = true");
        }
    }
}
Expected output
list, dupes kept     = [NUT-3, BOLT-7, NUT-3]
hashset size         = 2
linkedhashset        = [NUT-3, BOLT-7]
treeset, sorted      = [BOLT-7, NUT-3]
get missing key      = null
getOrDefault         = 0
containsKey NUT-3    = true
after restock        = 17
List.of is immutable = true

Note what is not printed: the HashSet's contents. Its iteration order is unspecified and may differ between JVM versions, so printing it in a test is how you get a suite that passes locally and fails in CI. Only the size is meaningful. LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order; TreeSet sorts.

Gotchas
  • map.get() returning null is ambiguous. It means either "no such key" or "the key maps to null". Use containsKey to distinguish, or getOrDefault to stop caring.
  • Unboxing a missing value throws. int n = onHand.get("NOPE"); compiles and throws NullPointerException. getOrDefault(key, 0) is the fix.
  • List.of and Map.of are immutable and reject nulls. Great as constants, wrong as a starting point for something you will mutate — wrap in new ArrayList<>(…) for that.
  • Keys must have correct equals/hashCode, and should be immutable. See section 10 for what breaks otherwise.
  • Declare the interface, construct the implementation. List<String> picks = new ArrayList<>() lets you swap the implementation without touching callers.
  • Size the collection if you know the count. new ArrayList<>(10_000) avoids a dozen grow-and-copy cycles.

Check yourself

1.You need to record which SKUs a picker has already visited on this run, and ask "seen this one?" tens of thousands of times. Order never matters. What do you use?

C. Membership testing is exactly what a hash set is for: O(1) contains and free deduplication.

A and D both scan the whole list — O(n) per check, so O(n²) overall, which is the classic reason a nightly job that was fine with 100 SKUs takes hours with 100,000. B works and is O(log n), but you are paying for sorted order you explicitly do not need.

2.A test asserts set.toString() equals "[BOLT-7, NUT-3]". It passes locally and fails on the build server. The set is a HashSet. Why, and what is the right fix?

B. Nothing guarantees HashSet iteration order — it falls out of hash values and table size, and can differ across JVM versions and vendors. The assertion was testing an implementation detail. Assert what you actually care about: that the set contains those two elements and has size 2.

A is a real cause of other cross-machine failures — date and case formatting — but not this one. C would more likely give a ConcurrentModificationException or corruption, not a stable-but-different order. D cannot be done to a HashSet in place; copying to a sorted structure just to satisfy an assertion is the tail wagging the dog — if order matters, choose an ordered type in the production code.

Section 13

Generics basics

Generics move a whole class of errors from runtime to compile time. List<Product> tells the compiler what goes in, so it can reject anything else and insert the casts on the way out for you. Before Java 5 every collection held Object and every read needed a hand-written cast that might fail.

The one thing to internalise now is erasure: generics exist for the compiler and are erased from the bytecode. At runtime a List<String> is just a List. That is why the guarantees are only as good as your willingness to keep the compiler informed.

What a raw type costs you

javaRawTypes.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class RawTypes {
    @SuppressWarnings({ "rawtypes", "unchecked" })
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List raw = new ArrayList();     // raw type: the compiler stops helping
        raw.add("BOLT-7");
        raw.add(42);                    // accepted without complaint
 
        for (Object o : raw) System.out.println("element: " + o);
 
        List<String> skus = raw;        // unchecked assignment, only a warning
        System.out.println("first : " + skus.get(0));
        System.out.println("second: " + skus.get(1));
    }
}
Expected output
element: BOLT-7
element: 42
first : BOLT-7
Then it throws
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException:
        class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String
        at RawTypes.main(RawTypes.java:15)

The failure lands on line 15 — a println that looks entirely innocent — while the actual mistake was on line 9, possibly in a different class written months earlier. skus.get(1) is declared to return String, so the compiler inserted a cast there; the cast is the first moment anyone checks. This distance between cause and symptom is what generics exist to remove. Declare List<String> from the start and line 9 fails to compile.

Treat unchecked warnings as errors

Every step above was legal Java and every step produced a warning. Compile with -Xlint:all -Werror and this code stops building. Reach for @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") only on the narrowest possible scope, and only when you have personally proved the cast is safe.

Writing a generic type

interface Repository<T> {                 // T is a type parameter
    void save(T item);
    T findBySku(String sku);
}
 
class ProductRepository implements Repository<Product> {
    @Override public void save(Product item) { /* … */ }
    @Override public Product findBySku(String sku) { /* … */ return null; }
}
 
// A generic METHOD declares its own parameter, before the return type:
static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items) {
    T best = items.get(0);
    for (T item : items) if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) best = item;
    return best;
}

<T extends Comparable<T>> is a bounded parameter: it accepts any type that can be compared to itself, which is what lets the body call compareTo. By convention T is a type, E an element, K and V a key and value. Wildcards (? extends, ? super) and the PECS rule belong to Java Intermediate.

Consequences of erasure
  • No primitives. List<int> does not compile — use List<Integer> and accept the boxing, or a primitive-specialised library if it is hot.
  • new T() is impossible. The type is gone by runtime. Pass a factory or a Class<T> if you must construct one.
  • o instanceof List<String> does not compile. Only instanceof List<?> — there is nothing left to test against.
  • Overloads that differ only by type argument clash. f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>) erase to the same signature.
  • Generic arrays are not allowed. new T[10] is a compile error; arrays know their element type at runtime and generics do not, so the two cannot be reconciled. Use an ArrayList.

Check yourself

1.In the worked example, why does the exception point at line 15 rather than at line 9, where the wrong element was added?

B. At runtime the list is a plain List holding Objects, so add(42) is a perfectly ordinary operation. Because skus.get(1) is declared to yield a String, javac emits a checkcast at the call site — and that is where reality and the declaration finally meet.

A and C describe validation and laziness that ArrayList does not have; it stores references immediately and checks nothing. D is wrong — the loop reads elements as Object, which needs no cast, so it prints 42 quite happily.

2.Which of these compiles?

C. Nested type arguments are fine, and the diamond <> infers them from the declaration.

A fails because a type argument must be a reference type — Integer, not int. B fails because the type argument is erased, so there is nothing to test; instanceof List<?> is the legal form. D fails on new T[] — an array stores its element type at runtime, which erasure has already thrown away, so the array could not enforce anything.

Section 14

Packages and access modifiers

A package is a namespace and a unit of access control. The declaration must be the first statement in the file, and the directory structure has to match: package com.acme.inventory; lives in com/acme/inventory/. Package names are reverse domain names to keep them globally unique.

Four access levels control who may see a member. The one people get wrong is the one you get by writing nothing at all.

Who can see what

Pick a modifier and a caller
Access matrix: modifier by caller location
ModifierSame classSame packageSubclass, other packageAnywhere
privateyesnonono
no modifieryesyesnono
protectedyesyesyesno
publicyesyesyesyes
Two things the table cannot show
  • There is no package keyword for access. Omitting a modifier is the declaration — the level is called package-private. Writing nothing is a decision, not a default you have deferred.
  • protected is narrower than it looks. A subclass in another package may access a protected member only through a reference of its own type (or a subtype), not through a bare superclass reference. other.shippingInCents() where other is declared Product will not compile inside Girder, even though Girder inherits it.

Encapsulation in practice

public class Order {
    private final String id;                       // nobody can reassign it
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    private Status status = Status.DRAFT;
 
    public Order(String id) {
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
    }
 
    public void addLine(OrderLine line) {          // the ONLY way lines change
        if (status != Status.DRAFT) throw new IllegalStateException("order is " + status);
        lines.add(line);
    }
 
    public List<OrderLine> lines() {
        return List.copyOf(lines);                 // defensive copy, not the field
    }
}

Line 12 is the part people skip. Returning the lines field directly would hand callers a live, mutable reference to internal state — they could add lines to a shipped order and bypass the check in addLine entirely. List.copyOf returns an immutable snapshot, so the invariant survives contact with the outside world. Making the field final only stops reassignment of the reference; it does nothing to stop mutation of what it points at.

Gotchas
  • One public top-level class per file, named after the file. Additional non-public classes in the same file are legal but are usually better off as nested or separate types.
  • Access is per class, not per object. A method of Order can read other.status on a different Order instance — which is how equals works at all.
