  • Start private and widen only when forced. Widening later is easy; narrowing a member other people already call is a breaking change.
  • Getters and setters for every field are not encapsulation. A setStatus that skips the state machine is a public field wearing a disguise. Expose operations — ship(), cancel() — not fields.
  • Wildcard imports hide clashes. import java.util.*; plus import java.sql.*; makes Date ambiguous and the file stops compiling. Import explicitly.

Check yourself

1.A field is declared int qty; with no modifier. Which callers can read it?

B. That is package-private. The unit of trust is the package, so any class sitting in the same one has full access — including classes someone else adds to that package later.

A is the most common wrong answer; private must be written explicitly. C is how it works in some other languages, not Java. D describes protected, which is strictly wider — it adds out-of-package subclasses on top of package access.

2.lines is private final, and lines() returns the field directly. A caller does order.lines().clear(). What happens?

C. The getter handed out a live reference to internal state, so the caller is now mutating the order's own list. Every invariant addLine protects is bypassed. Return List.copyOf(lines) — or better, expose no getter at all and add the operation the caller actually needs.

A confuses the field's access with the method's: lines() is public and hands the reference out legitimately. B is the crucial misunderstanding — final prevents reassigning the variable, never mutation of the object it refers to. D invents a defensive copy Java does not make for you.

Put it together

Hands-on lab: build the InventoryService

Six steps, each exercising something from the sections above. Write each one before opening the solution — reading a solution you have not attempted teaches almost nothing. Work in a single directory; every step compiles on its own with javac *.java.

Starter
mkdir inventory-lab && cd inventory-lab
# create Part.java, InventoryService.java and Lab.java as you go
javac *.java && java Lab

Everything is in the default package to keep the lab to three files. Real code would use package com.acme.inventory; and matching directories.

Step 1 — an encapsulated value type §8, §14

Write Part with a String sku and an int priceInCents. Both private final. The constructor must reject a null or blank SKU and a negative price with IllegalArgumentException. Expose read accessors, no setters.

Solution — step 1
public final class Part {
    private final String sku;
    private final int priceInCents;
 
    public Part(String sku, int priceInCents) {
        if (sku == null || sku.isBlank())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku must not be blank");
        if (priceInCents < 0)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("price must not be negative: " + priceInCents);
        this.sku = sku;
        this.priceInCents = priceInCents;
    }
 
    public String sku() { return sku; }
    public int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
}

Validating in the constructor means a Part can never exist in an invalid state — far stronger than checking at every use site. final on the class blocks the subclass that would break equals symmetry in step 2.

Step 2 — the equality contract §10

Two Parts are the same part when their SKUs match; price is not part of identity. Implement equals, hashCode and toString accordingly.

Solution — step 2
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Part other)) return false;
    return sku.equals(other.sku);
}
 
@Override public int hashCode() { return sku.hashCode(); }
 
@Override public String toString() {
    return "Part[" + sku + ", " + priceInCents + "c]";
}

Hash on exactly the field equals uses, and no other. Because sku is final, the hash can never drift after the part is used as a map key.

Step 3 — pick the right collections §12

InventoryService needs stock levels keyed by SKU, and a record of which SKUs have been picked this run, in the order picked. Choose both types and justify the choice to yourself before revealing.

Solution — step 3
private final Map<String, Integer> onHand = new HashMap<>();
private final Set<String> pickedThisRun = new LinkedHashSet<>();

HashMap for O(1) keyed lookup where iteration order is irrelevant. LinkedHashSet because the picks must be unique and reportable in order — a HashSet would lose the order and a List would allow the same SKU twice.

Step 4 — a domain exception §11

Add reserve(String sku, int qty). Throw IllegalArgumentException for a non-positive quantity, and a custom OutOfStockException when the request exceeds stock. Decide whether it should be checked or unchecked, and be able to defend it.

Solution — step 4
public class OutOfStockException extends Exception {   // CHECKED
    private final String sku;
    public OutOfStockException(String sku, int requested, int available) {
        super("cannot reserve " + requested + " of " + sku + "; only " + available + " on hand");
        this.sku = sku;
    }
    public String sku() { return sku; }
}
 
public void reserve(String sku, int qty) throws OutOfStockException {
    if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive: " + qty);
    int available = onHand.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
    if (qty > available) throw new OutOfStockException(sku, qty, available);
    onHand.put(sku, available - qty);
    pickedThisRun.add(sku);
}

Checked, because running out of stock is a normal business outcome the caller must decide about — back-order, substitute, or refuse — not a programming mistake. The bad quantity is unchecked, because that is a caller bug. Note getOrDefault rather than get: an unknown SKU is zero stock, and get would return null and throw on unboxing.

Step 5 — try-with-resources §11

Add loadFrom(Path) that reads lines of SKU,QTY and populates onHand, using try-with-resources so the reader always closes. Skip blank lines and lines starting with #.

Solution — step 5
public void loadFrom(Path file) throws IOException {
    try (BufferedReader in = Files.newBufferedReader(file)) {
        String line;
        while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) {
            line = line.strip();
            if (line.isEmpty() || line.startsWith("#")) continue;
            String[] parts = line.split(",");
            if (parts.length != 2)
                throw new IOException("malformed line: " + line);
            onHand.put(parts[0].strip(), Integer.parseInt(parts[1].strip()));
        }
    }
}

The reader closes whether the loop finishes, throws, or returns early. strip() rather than trim() so a non-breaking space in an exported file does not survive into a SKU. IOException is declared, not swallowed — the caller decides what a corrupt file means.

Step 6 — make it generic §13

Extract a Repository<T> interface with save(T), findById(String) and count(), then have a PartRepository implement Repository<Part>.

Solution — step 6
public interface Repository<T> {
    void save(T item);
    T findById(String id);
    int count();
}
 
public class PartRepository implements Repository<Part> {
    private final Map<String, Part> byS_ku = new HashMap<>();
    @Override public void save(Part item) { byS_ku.put(item.sku(), item); }
    @Override public Part findById(String id) { return byS_ku.get(id); }
    @Override public int count() { return byS_ku.size(); }
}

Callers get Part back with no cast and no possibility of a ClassCastException. findById returning null for a miss is the conventional shape here; Optional<Part> is the modern alternative and is covered in Java Intermediate.

The finished thing

All six steps assembled. This program is compiled and executed during the build of this page, so the output below is what it really prints.

javaLab.java
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
 
public class Lab {
 
    static final class Part {
        private final String sku;
        private final int priceInCents;
 
        Part(String sku, int priceInCents) {
            if (sku == null || sku.isBlank())
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku must not be blank");
            if (priceInCents < 0)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("price must not be negative: " + priceInCents);
            this.sku = sku;
            this.priceInCents = priceInCents;
        }
 
        String sku() { return sku; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
 
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            if (this == o) return true;
            if (!(o instanceof Part other)) return false;
            return sku.equals(other.sku);
        }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return sku.hashCode(); }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Part[" + sku + ", " + priceInCents + "c]"; }
    }
 
    static class OutOfStockException extends Exception {
        OutOfStockException(String sku, int requested, int available) {
            super("cannot reserve " + requested + " of " + sku + "; only " + available + " on hand");
        }
    }
 
    interface Repository<T> {
        void save(T item);
        T findById(String id);
        int count();
    }
 
    static final class PartRepository implements Repository<Part> {
        private final Map<String, Part> bySku = new HashMap<>();
        @Override public void save(Part item) { bySku.put(item.sku(), item); }
        @Override public Part findById(String id) { return bySku.get(id); }
        @Override public int count() { return bySku.size(); }
    }
 
    static final class InventoryService {
        private final Map<String, Integer> onHand = new HashMap<>();
        private final Set<String> pickedThisRun = new LinkedHashSet<>();
 
        void stock(String sku, int qty) { onHand.put(sku, onHand.getOrDefault(sku, 0) + qty); }
 
        void reserve(String sku, int qty) throws OutOfStockException {
            if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive: " + qty);
            int available = onHand.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
            if (qty > available) throw new OutOfStockException(sku, qty, available);
            onHand.put(sku, available - qty);
            pickedThisRun.add(sku);
        }
 
        int onHand(String sku) { return onHand.getOrDefault(sku, 0); }
        Set<String> picked() { return Set.copyOf(pickedThisRun); }
        String pickedInOrder() { return String.join(", ", pickedThisRun); }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PartRepository repo = new PartRepository();
        repo.save(new Part("BOLT-7", 80));
        repo.save(new Part("NUT-3", 25));
        repo.save(new Part("BOLT-7", 90));          // same sku: replaces, does not duplicate
        System.out.println("repo count      = " + repo.count());
        System.out.println("lookup          = " + repo.findById("BOLT-7"));
        System.out.println("equal by sku    = " + new Part("BOLT-7", 1).equals(new Part("BOLT-7", 999)));
 
        InventoryService inv = new InventoryService();
        inv.stock("BOLT-7", 10);
        inv.stock("NUT-3", 4);
 
        try {
            inv.reserve("BOLT-7", 3);
            inv.reserve("NUT-3", 4);
            inv.reserve("BOLT-7", 2);
            inv.reserve("NUT-3", 1);                 // NUT-3 is exhausted
        } catch (OutOfStockException e) {
            System.out.println("caught          = " + e.getMessage());
        }
 
        try {
            inv.reserve("BOLT-7", 0);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("bad qty         = " + e.getMessage());
        } catch (OutOfStockException e) {
            System.out.println("unreachable");
        }
 
        System.out.println("BOLT-7 on hand  = " + inv.onHand("BOLT-7"));
        System.out.println("picked in order = " + inv.pickedInOrder());
        System.out.println("unknown sku     = " + inv.onHand("NOPE"));
    }
}
Expected output
repo count      = 2
lookup          = Part[BOLT-7, 90c]
equal by sku    = true
caught          = cannot reserve 1 of NUT-3; only 0 on hand
bad qty         = qty must be positive: 0
BOLT-7 on hand  = 5
picked in order = BOLT-7, NUT-3
unknown sku     = 0
Extensions worth attempting
  • Add release(sku, qty) that returns stock and removes the SKU from pickedThisRun only when nothing of it remains reserved. You will need a second map — think about what breaks if you forget it.
  • Make reserve atomic across several SKUs: either all succeed or none do. What has to happen to pickedThisRun on rollback?
  • Give Part a Category enum and group the repository by it. Which Map type gives you categories in declaration order?

Rules that prevent most beginner bugs

  1. Compare objects with equals, never ==.
  2. Override equals and hashCode together, from the same fields.
  3. Write @Override every time you intend to override.
  4. Declare fields private; return copies of mutable internal state.
  5. Prefer the enhanced for; you cannot go out of bounds without a bound.
  6. Never concatenate strings in a loop — use StringBuilder.
  7. Never use double for money — use BigDecimal or integer cents.
  8. Never leave a catch block empty.
  9. Use try-with-resources for anything closeable.
  10. Parameterise your generics; treat unchecked warnings as errors.
  11. Declare the interface, construct the implementation.
  12. Prefer getOrDefault to get when a miss means zero.

Rehearsal

Interview questions

Twelve questions that actually get asked, with the answer a strong candidate gives. Say your answer out loud before opening the reveal — recognising an answer and being able to produce one are different skills.

Easy  1. What is the difference between the JDK, the JRE and the JVM?

The JVM executes bytecode; it is the specification and the process implementing it. The JRE is the JVM plus the standard class library — enough to run a program. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools, notably javac. Each contains the previous. Practically: install a JDK, since Java 11 there is no separate JRE download from most vendors, and if java works but javac does not, that is what has happened.

Easy  2. Why should you never compare strings with ==?

== compares references, not characters. It appears to work for literals because identical compile-time literals share one pooled instance — which is exactly what makes the bug dangerous, since it passes every test written with literals and fails the moment a string arrives from a file, socket, database or Scanner. Use equals, or Objects.equals when a side may be null.

Easy  3. Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Always pass-by-value. For reference types the reference is what gets copied, so the method can mutate the object you handed it, but reassigning the parameter has no effect on the caller's variable. That is why you cannot write a working swap(a, b) in Java. People call this "pass-by-reference" loosely; being precise about it is a good signal.

Medium  4. What happens if you override equals but not hashCode?

Every hash-based collection breaks. Two equal objects get different identity-derived hash codes and land in different buckets, so a HashSet stores both and contains with an equal instance returns false. Nothing throws — the JDK cannot detect the violation. The contract is that equal objects must return equal hash codes; the converse is not required, since collisions are unavoidable. Follow-up they often add: is a constant hashCode legal? Yes, and it is correct but degrades every lookup to a single bucket.

Medium  5. Checked versus unchecked exceptions — when do you use each?

Checked extends Exception and must be caught or declared; use it for conditions a correct program can still meet and should decide about — a missing file, a rejected payment, an out-of-stock item. Unchecked extends RuntimeException; use it for programming errors where the fix is to change the code — a null that should have been guarded, an argument violating a documented precondition. Error is a third category for JVM-level failures you should not catch at all.

Medium  6. ArrayList or LinkedList?

ArrayList, essentially always. The textbook claim that LinkedList inserts in O(1) ignores that you must first walk to the index, which is O(n) — so the total is the same, while ArrayList's shift is one System.arraycopy over contiguous, cache-friendly memory. LinkedList also pays an object header and two references per element. It wins only when inserting through an Iterator you already hold. For a queue or stack use ArrayDeque, not LinkedList.

Medium  7. Explain String immutability and why it was chosen.

A String's characters never change; every "modifying" method returns a new instance. The reasons: pooling is only safe if instances cannot change; hash codes can be cached, which makes String an excellent map key; instances are automatically thread-safe; and security-sensitive values such as file paths and class names cannot be mutated between a check and its use. The cost is allocation, which is why concatenating in a loop is O(n²) and StringBuilder exists.

Medium  8. What is autoboxing, and where does it bite?

Automatic conversion between primitives and their wrappers. Three traps: unboxing a null throws NullPointerException at an assignment that looks harmless; == on wrappers compares references, so it is true for values in the −128…127 cache and false outside it; and boxing in a loop allocates an object per iteration. Also overload resolution — list.remove(1) removes an index, list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes a value.

Hard  9. Give the full initialization order for a subclass instance.

On first active use of the class: superclass static fields and static blocks, then this class's. Then on every new: superclass instance fields and initializer blocks, superclass constructor body, this class's instance fields and initializer blocks, this class's constructor body. Within a level, source order. Two consequences worth volunteering: statics run once and lazily, not at JVM start; and because the superclass constructor runs before the subclass's fields are initialised, calling an overridable method from a constructor lets the override observe null and 0.

Hard  10. What is type erasure and what does it prevent?

Generic type arguments exist only at compile time and are erased from the bytecode, so a List<String> is a plain List at runtime. It was done for backward compatibility with pre-generics code. Consequences: no new T(), no new T[], no instanceof List<String>, no overloads differing only by type argument, and no primitive type arguments. It is also why a raw type can smuggle a wrong element in and the ClassCastException surfaces later, at the read, far from the cause.

Hard  11. Overloading versus overriding — and when is each resolved?

Overloading is same name, different parameter types, resolved by the compiler from the static types of the arguments, in three phases: exact and widening first, then boxing, then varargs. Overriding is a subclass replacing a superclass method with the same signature, resolved by the JVM from the object's runtime class. So one call site can be picked at compile time and dispatched at runtime, and mixing them up produces genuinely surprising behaviour — a common test is a method overloaded on Object and String called with a null, or with a variable declared Object holding a String.

Hard  12. What does try-with-resources do that finally does not?

Three things. It closes resources in reverse acquisition order automatically. It closes only what was successfully acquired, so if the second resource's constructor throws, the first is still closed and the second is not touched. And it suppresses rather than discards: if the body throws and close() also throws, the body's exception propagates and the close exception is attached, retrievable via getSuppressed(). The hand-written finally { in.close(); } pattern gets the last one backwards, replacing the real failure with the close failure — which is how the actual cause of an outage disappears.

Assessment

Self-assessment quiz

Sixteen questions covering all nine learning objectives. Answer every one, then submit — nothing is marked until you do, and the explanations stay hidden until then. Your answers are saved locally, so you can leave and come back.

1.A colleague can run java -version but not javac. What do they have?

C. The JRE runs programs; the JDK adds the tools to build them. B is impossible — a JRE contains the JVM, so having the JVM means having at least a JRE. A and D invent causes for what is simply the normal JRE layout.

2.int qty = Integer.MAX_VALUE; qty++; — what is qty?

B. Two's-complement wraparound, with no diagnostic. C is what Math.incrementExact would do and is what you want when overflow matters. A is saturating arithmetic, which Java does not have. D never happens on assignment back into an int.

3.Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; — what are a == b and a.equals(b)?

C. 1000 is outside the −128…127 Integer cache, so two distinct objects are allocated and == compares references. equals compares values. With 100 instead of 1000, A would be correct — that inconsistency is the whole trap.

4.What is -7 % 2 in Java?

A. Java's % takes its sign from the left operand, so it can be negative. B is Math.floorMod(-7, 2), which is what you want when wrapping an array index. C is -7 / 2.

5.String s = "BOLT"; s.concat("-7"); System.out.println(s);

D. Strings are immutable; concat returns a new string that nothing captured. A assumes mutation in place. C is at most a warning, never an error — which is why this slips through.

6.A SKU read from a socket fails an == comparison against the literal "BOLT-7", though both print identically. Why?

B. == compares references, and the pooled literal is not the same object as the one built from bytes. C is wrong — == is perfectly well defined, just not what you meant. A and D invent mechanisms; Java strings carry no terminator.

7.Building a 10,000-line CSV with report += line + "," inside a loop is slow. Why?

C. Use a StringBuilder. Note the boundary: a + chain in a single expression compiles to one efficient concatenation and needs no rewriting — the problem is specifically re-concatenating across iterations. A, B and D are invented mechanisms.

8.You must test membership tens of thousands of times, order irrelevant. Which collection?

B. O(1) contains. A and C scan linearly, giving O(n²) overall — the classic reason a job fine at 100 items crawls at 100,000. D works at O(log n) but charges you for sorted order you do not need.

9.A test asserting hashSet.toString() passes locally and fails in CI. The correct fix is…

A. The assertion was testing an implementation detail. B hides it rather than fixing it, and order can change between versions of one vendor anyway. C addresses concurrency, which is not what is happening. D is a real cause of other cross-machine failures — date and case formatting — but not this one.

10.Product overrides equals on sku only. Two same-SKU products go into a HashSet. Most likely result?

D. Without hashCode, equal objects hash to different buckets, so equals is never consulted. A needs hashCode overridden too. B never happens — the JDK cannot detect the violation. C is self-contradictory: the same mismatch that stored the duplicate also breaks lookup.

11.Running out of stock is a normal business outcome the caller must decide about. What kind of exception?

B. A correct program can hit it and must handle it, which is exactly the case checked exceptions model. A suits programming errors such as a negative quantity. C is reserved for JVM-level failures. D pushes the problem to a NullPointerException somewhere less informative.

12.try (A a = new A(); B b = new B()) — A constructs, then B's constructor throws. What is closed?

C. Only successfully acquired resources are closed, in reverse order. A would leak A. B would call close() on a never-assigned reference. This is exactly the case hand-written finally blocks get wrong.

13.Given f(int), f(Integer) and f(int...), which runs for f(7)?

A. Phase 1 allows only exact and widening matches, finds f(int), and stops. B needs boxing (phase 2) and C needs varargs (phase 3), neither of which is reached. D would require two candidates in the same phase.

14.A raw List got an Integer added, was assigned to List<String>, and throws ClassCastException at a get. Why there and not at the add?

C. At runtime it is a plain List of Object. Because get is declared to return String, javac emits a checkcast there. D is close but wrong in attribution — the JVM knows nothing about generics; the compiler inserted the cast. A and B describe behaviour that does not exist.

15.A field declared int qty; with no modifier is visible to…

B. That is package-private, the level you get by writing nothing. A requires an explicit private — the most common wrong answer. D describes protected, which is strictly wider.

16.Which safely remove elements while walking a list? Select all that apply.

A and C. B throws ConcurrentModificationException. D is worse than throwing: removing at i shifts everything left, the loop increments i, and the element that slid into that slot is skipped — so two adjacent matches silently leave one behind.

Reference

Glossary

Thirty terms, each linked back to the section that introduces it. The same entries drive the flashcard deck below — one list, two ways to use it.

Flashcards

Autoboxing
Automatic conversion between a primitive and its wrapper class, inserted by the compiler. Convenient, but the source of null-unboxing crashes and == surprises. §2
Bytecode
The portable instruction set javac emits into .class files. Not machine code — it targets the abstract JVM, which is why one build runs everywhere. §1
Checked exception
An Exception that is not a RuntimeException. The compiler forces you to catch it or declare it. Models conditions a correct program can still meet. §11
Class loader
The JVM component that finds a .class file, links it, and makes the type available. Runs on first active use, not at startup. §1
ConcurrentModificationException
Thrown when a collection is structurally changed while being iterated. Despite the name, usually a single thread doing it to itself. §5
Defensive copy
Returning a copy of internal mutable state rather than the field itself, so callers cannot reach past your invariants. §14
Dynamic dispatch
Choosing which overridden method body runs from the object's runtime class, not the declared type of the variable. §8
Encapsulation
Keeping state private and exposing operations that enforce the rules, so an object cannot be put into an invalid condition from outside. §8
Enhanced for loop
for (T x : items). Uses an iterator underneath, and cannot go out of bounds because you never write a bound. §5
Erasure
Generic type arguments exist only at compile time and are removed from the bytecode. Why new T(), new T[] and instanceof List<String> are all impossible. §13
equals/hashCode contract
Objects that are equals must return the same hashCode. Break it and every hash-based collection gives wrong answers silently. §10
final
Prevents reassignment of a variable, overriding of a method, or subclassing of a class. It does not make the referenced object immutable. §14
Immutability
An object's state cannot change after construction. String is the canonical example; every "modifying" method returns a new instance. §3
Instance initializer
A bare { … } block in a class body. Runs on every construction, after the implicit super() and before the constructor body. §9
Integer cache
Integer.valueOf returns shared instances for −128…127. Why == on boxed values is true for small numbers and false for large ones. §2
Interface
A contract with no instance state. A class may implement many, which is why it is the default choice for expressing a capability. §8
JIT compiler
Compiles frequently executed bytecode to native code while the program runs. Why JVM benchmarks need a warm-up phase. §1
JDK / JRE / JVM
Development kit (adds javac and tools) ⊃ runtime environment (JVM plus class library) ⊃ the virtual machine that executes bytecode. §1
Overloading
Several methods with one name and different parameter types. Resolved by the compiler in three phases: exact/widening, then boxing, then varargs. §7
Overriding
A subclass replacing an inherited method with the same signature. Resolved by the JVM at runtime. Always mark it @Override. §8
Package-private
The access level you get by writing no modifier at all: visible to every class in the same package, and nothing else. §14
Pass-by-value
Java's only calling convention. For references the reference is copied, so a method can mutate your object but cannot repoint your variable. §7
Polymorphism
Writing code against a supertype and having it work for every subtype, with the actual behaviour selected at runtime. §8
Primitive
One of the eight non-object value types. Cannot be null, cannot go directly into a collection, and has a fixed bit width. §2
Raw type
A generic type used without its type argument, e.g. plain List. Legal for backward compatibility; switches off the compiler's help. §13
Short-circuit evaluation
&& and || skip the right operand when the left already decides the result. Load-bearing for null and divide-by-zero guards. §4
static
Belongs to the class rather than any instance. One copy shared by everything, initialised once on first active use. §9
String pool
A JVM-managed set of shared String instances holding compile-time literals and interned strings. Why == sometimes appears to work. §3
Try-with-resources
try (R r = …). Closes what it acquired, in reverse order, and suppresses rather than discards a secondary exception from close(). §11
Unchecked exception
A RuntimeException subclass. Needs no declaration, and models a programming error whose fix is to change the code. §11

Where to go next

Further reading

Primary sources only — specifications, official documentation, and the two books that are actually worth the shelf space. These are links, but nothing on this page loads them; the module remains fully offline.

Specifications and official docs

  • The Java Language Specification, Java SE 21 Edition — the final word on every rule in this module. Chapter 5 (conversions and promotions) and §15.12 (method invocation) are where the overload-resolution phases are defined.
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/index.html
  • The Java Virtual Machine Specification, Java SE 21 Edition — class loading, linking, initialization order, and the bytecode instruction set.
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se21/html/index.html
  • Java SE 21 API documentation — the Javadoc. Read the class-level notes on HashMap, ArrayList and String; they document the performance characteristics this module summarises.
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/index.html
  • Object.equals and Object.hashCode Javadoc — the contract itself, stated in about two hundred words. Worth reading in the original.
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html
  • The Java Tutorials — Oracle's introductory trail. Uneven, occasionally dated, but the Collections and Generics trails are solid.
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/

Books

  • Effective Java, Joshua Bloch, 3rd edition — the single most useful Java book. Items 10 through 14 cover equals, hashCode, toString, Comparable and clone in far more depth than section 10 here. Read it after this module, not before.
  • Java: A Beginner's Guide, Herbert Schildt — a conventional ground-up introduction if you want a second explanation of the same fundamentals in a different voice.
  • Java Concurrency in Practice, Brian Goetz et al. — the standard reference for the threading material in Java Advanced. Predates virtual threads but the model it teaches is unchanged.

Tools worth knowing early

Useful JDK tools and what they are for
ToolUse it to
jshellTry a snippet without writing a class or a main. The fastest way to settle an argument about what Java does.
javap -cDisassemble a .class file. Shows you the string concatenation the compiler generated, and that generics really are erased.
javac -Xlint:all -WerrorTurn every warning into a build failure. Catches raw types and unchecked casts before they reach production.
jcmd / jstackInspect a running JVM — thread dumps, heap info, GC statistics.
Next module

The course continues in two further modules, both built on the same warehouse example.

Java Intermediate picks up exactly where this stops: generics in depth (wildcards, PECS, bounded types), nested and inner classes, interfaces and enums in full, lambdas and method references, streams and collectors, Optional, records, sealed types with pattern matching and switch expressions, Comparator and immutability, the internals of HashMap and ArrayList, java.time, and file I/O.

Java Advanced then covers the runtime: threads and the Java memory model, locks and concurrent collections, executors, CompletableFuture and virtual threads, garbage collection and JVM tuning, class loading, reflection and annotations, the module system, and performance measurement. Take the quiz above first; if you scored below 65%, the sections you missed are worth a second pass before moving on.
